messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos, a 75-year-old Latin American man, has been profoundly affected by his experience during a devastating wildfire that swept through his hometown two years ago. A QA Engineer by profession, Carlos and his wife managed to escape the inferno in their small home, but not without enduring harrowing moments of smoke inhalation and watching flames consume their surroundings. In the weeks following the disaster, every time Carlos smelled smoke or saw fire, he was transported back to that terrifying day. The mere sight of fire or flames triggered an intense physical reaction—his heart would race, his palms would sweat, and he felt jumpy and easily startled. This hyperalertness extended even further when similar weather conditions returned, as if the threat of another wildfire could arise at any moment. Carlos found himself increasingly dwelling on what he might have done differently to prevent or mitigate the situation. He ruminated endlessly about whether they should have evacuated sooner or taken different precautions. These thoughts were so intrusive that he tried to push them out of his mind, but the attempts only made him more anxious and consumed by guilt. The cycle of distress worsened over time. Whenever Carlos encountered a trigger—such as the smell of smoke from barbecues in the neighborhood or the sight of flames during Fourth of July celebrations—he found himself reverting to self-blame rumination and preventive ruminations about how he could have done more. This self-critical narrative heightened his sense of threat, making him even more hypervigilant and prone to startling easily at sudden sounds. This hyperalertness had seeped into every aspect of Carlos’s life, including his work environment. The smell of burning electronics or the occasional fire alarm test at the office would send him into a panic. He began avoiding certain tasks and areas that might trigger these memories, leading to increased workplace stress and strained relationships with colleagues who didn’t understand why he was so reluctant to perform certain duties. Despite attempts to suppress these thoughts, Carlos’s preoccupation grew worse, and the triggers seemed more potent than ever. The physical reactivity to reminders of the wildfire intensified, making him feel perpetually on edge. This heightened state of threat monitoring led him to become even more vigilant and jumpy, further fueling his maladaptive strategies. What frightened Carlos most was the fear that another disaster could strike at any moment, especially during weather conditions similar to those of the original event. The constant anticipation of danger made him question whether he could ever feel safe again. The strain on his mental health became unbearable when a minor incident at work—a colleague setting off a fire alarm—triggered a full-blown panic attack that left Carlos feeling both physically and emotionally drained. Realizing he needed help, Carlos finally sought therapy. Carlos is most afraid of the unpredictability and ongoing threat of another disaster. However, he hopes to regain control over his life and find ways to manage his triggers without falling into self-destructive patterns of rumination and avoidance. He wants to feel safe in his home and workplace again, free from the constant fear that haunts him every day.
